records.title: Malignant spinal cord compression
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Epidural tumour compressing the spinal cord or cauda equina. Presents with new or worsening back pain, leg weakness, a sensory level, or bladder or bowel change in a patient with cancer. Treat before the patient loses the ability to walk. Dexamethasone 16 mg (oral or equivalent IV) as soon as MSCC is suspected, with PPI cover; do not wait for imaging. Whole-spine MRI within 24 h (CT with contrast if MRI is contraindicated). Image the whole spine; lesions are often at more than one level. Flat bed rest and spinal precautions until spinal stability is assessed. Refer the same day to oncology and to spinal surgery or radiation oncology. Assess and record whether the patient can walk; this predicts outcome. Recognise Back pain is often the first symptom and may precede neurological signs by weeks; it is worse lying down, on straining or at night. It progresses to limb weakness, a sensory level and gait disturbance, and later to urinary retention or incontinence and reduced anal tone. The thoracic spine is the most common site. A motor deficit that develops over less than 24–48 h has a worse prognosis and needs faster diagnosis than one that develops over more than 7 days. Bladder and bowel signs are late; do not wait for them. Most common primaries: breast, prostate, lung, myeloma, renal. Confirm Whole-spine MRI within 24 h of suspected MSCC is the investigation of choice; whole-spine CT with contrast if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. Image the entire spine: compression is at more than one level in about a third of cases, and a second site changes the plan. Obtain a tissue diagnosis if the primary is unknown, but do not delay steroids or definitive treatment for the biopsy when the cord is threatened. Manage Corticosteroid: dexamethasone 16 mg (oral or equivalent parenteral) as soon as MSCC is suspected, then 16 mg daily while awaiting surgery or radiotherapy, with gastric protection and glucose monitoring; taper once definitive treatment has started. Stop it if imaging excludes MSCC. A 10 mg IV loading dose is common practice but is not part of the NICE regimen. Surgery or radiotherapy: in the Patchell RCT, decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy preserved and restored walking better than radiotherapy alone (walking after treatment 84% vs 57%; among patients unable to walk at entry, walking regained 62% vs 19%). Prefer surgery for a single area of compression, spinal instability, an unknown primary needing tissue, radioresistant histology, or a deficit despite or after prior radiotherapy, in patients fit for surgery with a reasonable prognosis. Radiotherapy for patients who are not surgical candidates, radiosensitive tumours, disease at several levels, or poor performance status. Systemic therapy can be first-line, alongside the above, for highly chemosensitive or hormone-sensitive disease (for example lymphoma, germ cell tumours, some prostate cancer). Catheterise urinary retention; VTE prophylaxis; pressure-area and bowel care; analgesia. Disposition & escalation Admit and discuss the same day with spinal surgery and radiation oncology (many centres have an MSCC coordinator or pathway). Ability to walk before treatment is the strongest predictor of walking afterwards: most patients treated while still walking remain able to walk, and few recover once paraplegic. Aim for definitive treatment within 24 h of diagnosis when the cord is threatened. Pitfalls Waiting for bladder or bowel signs; by then cord function is often lost. Imaging only the symptomatic level and missing compression higher up. Withholding steroids until the MRI, or omitting gastric protection and glucose monitoring. Referring the next day instead of at the time of suspicion. Related: raised ICP and brain metastasis emergencies (this module) for steroids in oedema. NICE NG234 Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression (2023) · Patchell RA et al, Lancet 2005;366:643–648 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(05)66954-1; PMID 16112300). ESMO Handbook ch. 7.

records.title: Superior vena cava obstruction
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Obstruction of flow in the superior vena cava. Presents with swelling of the face, neck or arms, distended neck and chest-wall veins, dyspnoea and plethora; usually from lung cancer or lymphoma. Airway and cerebral signs, not the facial swelling, decide how urgent it is. Look for stridor or airway compromise and for cerebral signs (confusion, reduced consciousness, visual change from laryngeal or cerebral oedema). Either makes it an emergency. Sit the patient up; give oxygen. Obtain tissue first unless airway or cerebral compromise needs immediate treatment; treatment depends on the histology. Endovascular stenting for severe or life-threatening obstruction (Yale grade 3–4). It gives the fastest relief and does not need a diagnosis. Recognise Facial and neck swelling, dyspnoea and a feeling of fullness, distended neck and chest-wall collateral veins, facial plethora, cough; worse on bending forward or lying flat. Onset is usually gradual as collaterals develop, so most presentations are urgent but not immediately life-threatening. A minority are dangerous: stridor or airway oedema, and cerebral oedema (headache, confusion, obtundation), from an SVC that occludes faster than collaterals can form. These take precedence over the usual rule of biopsy first. Most causes are malignant: non-small-cell and small-cell lung cancer, non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Also consider thrombosis related to a catheter or device. Confirm Contrast CT of the thorax shows the level, extent and cause of the obstruction and guides both biopsy and stenting. Obtain a histological diagnosis (sputum or pleural cytology, nodal or bronchoscopic biopsy, image-guided core biopsy) before treatment. Management depends on the disease, and treatment without a diagnosis can prevent the diagnosis of a curable cancer (for example lymphoma, small-cell lung cancer, germ cell tumour). Manage Endovascular stenting gives the fastest symptom relief and is the treatment of choice for severe or life-threatening SVCO. It does not depend on histology, so it can come before the diagnosis when symptoms are urgent. Treatment of the tumour by histology: chemotherapy (with or without a stent) for chemosensitive disease (small-cell lung cancer, lymphoma, germ cell tumour); radiotherapy for non-small-cell lung cancer and other less chemosensitive tumours. Anticoagulation if the obstruction is thrombotic or a stent is placed (local protocol). Corticosteroids are often given, but evidence is weak and benefit is uncertain except in steroid-responsive tumours (lymphoma) or to limit oedema during radiotherapy. They do not replace definitive treatment. Head elevation and oxygen are supportive only. Grade: Yale (Yu) system G0 radiographic obstruction, asymptomatic. G1 mild: head and neck oedema, plethora, cyanosis. G2 moderate: oedema with functional impairment (mild dysphagia, cough, mild visual disturbance). G3 severe: cerebral oedema (mild headache, dizziness) or laryngeal oedema, or reduced cardiac reserve (syncope on bending). G4 life-threatening: significant cerebral oedema (confusion, obtundation) or laryngeal oedema (stridor), or significant haemodynamic compromise. G5 fatal. At grade 3–4, urgent stenting comes before the biopsy. Disposition & escalation Grade 3–4 (airway or cerebral signs, haemodynamic compromise): monitored bed, urgent interventional radiology for stenting, anaesthetic or ITU input for a threatened airway. Grade 1–2: rapid work-up to a tissue diagnosis, then treatment for the specific disease. True emergencies are a minority. Pitfalls Radiotherapy before biopsy: it can make a lymphoma or small-cell lung cancer impossible to classify and lose the chance of curative treatment. Treating every SVCO as life-threatening. Most cases are urgent, not peri-arrest; airway and cerebral signs, not facial swelling, set the urgency. Missing a catheter-associated thrombus as the cause. Yu JB, Wilson LD, Detterbeck FC, J Thorac Oncol 2008;3:811–814 (Yale/Yu classification & management algorithm; PMID 18670297). ESMO Handbook ch. 3.

records.title: Cardiac tamponade / malignant pericardial effusion
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Pericardial fluid raises intrapericardial pressure and restricts cardiac filling, causing obstructive shock. Dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypotension and raised JVP in a patient with cancer; it can progress to PEA arrest. Echocardiography now. It makes the diagnosis (effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium or ventricle, a plethoric IVC) and guides drainage. Look for decompensation: hypotension, tachycardia, raised JVP (Beck's triad), pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg). Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis for haemodynamic compromise; this is the definitive treatment. Do not delay it for a full oncological work-up. Give IV fluids while preparing to drain. Avoid intubation and positive-pressure ventilation if possible; they can precipitate arrest in tamponade. Recognise Progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, fatigue, chest discomfort; on examination tachycardia, hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins) is specific but insensitive: the full triad is uncommon, and its absence does not exclude tamponade. Tamponade is defined by its haemodynamic effect, not by the size of the effusion. A small effusion that accumulates quickly can cause tamponade when a large chronic one does not. Common in advanced lung and breast cancer, lymphoma and melanoma; also after radiation pericarditis and, rarely, with immunotherapy. Confirm Echocardiography is the most useful test. It confirms and sizes the effusion and shows tamponade physiology: diastolic collapse of the right atrium and then the right ventricle, a plethoric IVC that does not collapse, and respiratory variation in transvalvular flow. Effusion size on echo in diastole: mild <10 mm, moderate 10–20 mm, large >20 mm. ECG may show low voltages and electrical alternans; chest X-ray a globular heart. Send drained fluid for cytology. Manage Pericardiocentesis (echo-guided or fluoroscopic) is indicated for tamponade, for symptomatic large effusions, and when a neoplastic cause is suspected; it is diagnostic and therapeutic. Leave a catheter for extended drainage; this greatly reduces reaccumulation compared with a single aspiration. While preparing: IV fluid to support preload; a vasopressor if needed. Avoid positive-pressure ventilation where possible; it reduces venous return and can cause arrest in compensated tamponade. Preventing recurrence: extended catheter drainage, or a surgical pericardial window (subxiphoid or thoracoscopic) for recurrent or loculated effusions. Intrapericardial sclerosing or cytotoxic agents are an option but cause chest pain and constriction, and are used selectively. Systemic treatment of the underlying cancer gives lasting control. Disposition & escalation Monitored bed, HDU or ICU; involve cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery. Recurrence rates guide escalation: reaccumulation after a single pericardiocentesis is common (about 38% in pooled series), against about 10–12% with extended catheter drainage, sclerosis or balloon pericardiotomy, and under about 7% after a surgical window. A recurrent malignant effusion therefore needs a window or extended drainage, not repeat aspiration. Pitfalls Judging by effusion size: a small, fast effusion can cause tamponade; a large, slow one may not. Intubating a hypotensive patient with tamponade before drainage: risk of peri-arrest. Aggressive diuresis or vasodilators: they reduce preload and worsen the obstruction. Single aspiration and discharge in malignant disease: plan for reaccumulation. 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921–2964 (PMID 26320112) · malignant pericardial effusion recurrence rates from pooled observational data (systematic review, PMC11357784). ESMO Handbook ch. 1.

records.title: Raised intracranial pressure & brain-metastasis crises
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Mass effect, vasogenic oedema or haemorrhage from brain metastases raises ICP. Headache, vomiting, drowsiness, focal deficit, seizure; herniation leads to arrest. Recognise herniation: falling GCS, new pupillary asymmetry or a fixed dilated pupil, Cushing response (hypertension and bradycardia), abnormal posturing. This is a neurosurgical emergency. Airway and breathing first; nurse head-up at about 30° with the head midline; treat hypoxia and hypercapnia. Dexamethasone for vasogenic oedema: up to 16 mg/day for severe raised-ICP symptoms (4–8 mg/day for milder mass-effect symptoms), with PPI cover. For impending herniation: hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 15–30 min, or 3% hypertonic saline) and call neurosurgery immediately. Recognise Raised ICP: headache (worse on waking, coughing or lying flat), nausea and vomiting, increasing drowsiness, papilloedema and developing focal deficits. A seizure may be the first sign. Signs of herniation (falling consciousness, a new dilated or unreactive pupil, the Cushing response of hypertension with bradycardia, extensor posturing) mean decompensation and need immediate action. Sudden deterioration suggests haemorrhage into a tumour (melanoma, renal, choriocarcinoma, thyroid) or obstructive hydrocephalus. Confirm Urgent CT head (with contrast, or MRI where possible) for the number, size and site of metastases, midline shift, hydrocephalus and haemorrhage. In a patient who is herniating, do not delay hyperosmolar therapy or the neurosurgical call for imaging; treat and scan at the same time. Manage Corticosteroid for vasogenic oedema: dexamethasone 4–8 mg/day for mild to moderate mass-effect symptoms, up to 16 mg/day for severe or raised-ICP symptoms. Higher doses add toxicity without extra benefit in less severe disease, so reserve them. Steroids are not indicated for asymptomatic metastases. Give gastric protection and monitor glucose; taper to the lowest effective dose. A 10 mg IV loading dose is common practice but is not a fixed guideline figure. Hyperosmolar therapy for herniation or critical ICP: mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 15–30 min, or 3% hypertonic saline as an alternative. It buys time until decompression and is not a treatment on its own. Seizures: treat active seizures (a benzodiazepine, then a loading dose of an antiepileptic). Do not give prophylactic antiepileptics to patients with brain metastases who have not had a seizure; routine prophylaxis is not recommended. Definitive control: urgent neurosurgery (resection of a dominant or haemorrhagic lesion; CSF diversion for hydrocephalus) and/or radiotherapy (SRS for limited disease, whole-brain radiotherapy in selected cases); systemic therapy where the disease is highly responsive. Airway protection, head-up positioning, normocapnia; brief controlled hyperventilation only while awaiting theatre. Disposition & escalation Herniation or critically raised ICP: immediate neurosurgical referral, ICU or HDU, airway management. Control oedema with steroids and decide definitive local treatment (surgery or radiotherapy) with neuro-oncology and radiation oncology, taking into account performance status, extent of systemic disease and prognosis. Pitfalls Prophylactic antiepileptics in a patient who has not had a seizure: no benefit, with interactions and toxicity. Dexamethasone 16 mg for every patient: match the dose to symptom severity; excess steroid causes myopathy, hyperglycaemia and infection. Using mannitol or hyperventilation as more than a temporary measure before surgical decompression. Missing haemorrhage into a tumour or hydrocephalus as the cause of sudden deterioration. Related: MSCC (this module) for steroids in oedema; immunotherapy-related neurotoxicity and its steroid doses are in Tox. Chang SM et al (Congress of Neurological Surgeons; ASCO/SNO endorsement), J Clin Oncol 2019;37:1130–1135 — anticonvulsant prophylaxis & steroid use in metastatic brain tumours (DOI 10.1200/JCO.18.02085) · hyperosmolar dosing per Neurocritical Care Society Emergency Neurological Life Support (ICP/herniation). ESMO Handbook ch. 8.

records.title: Malignant central airway obstruction / stridor
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Tumour narrowing the trachea or main bronchi, from within the lumen or by external compression. Causes positional dyspnoea, stridor and monophonic wheeze; a compensated airway can close suddenly. Sit the patient up; high-flow humidified O₂; heliox (helium–oxygen) to improve flow through the narrowing while definitive treatment is arranged. High-dose corticosteroid for oedema around the tumour; nebulised adrenaline as a temporary measure. Call interventional pulmonology or ENT, and anaesthesia, immediately. Definitive relief is urgent rigid bronchoscopy with debulking, with or without a stent. Do not sedate, paralyse, or lie the patient flat before the airway is controlled. Recognise Stridor (fixed obstruction within the chest may give expiratory stridor or monophonic wheeze), dyspnoea on exertion and then with position, cough, haemoptysis. Usually from central lung, thyroid, oesophageal or mediastinal nodal disease: tumour within the lumen, external compression, or both. Signs of imminent arrest: exhaustion, use of accessory muscles, a quiet chest, falling SpO₂ with rising CO₂. Confirm If the patient is deteriorating, call the interventional team before imaging. When stable: flexible nasendoscopy or bronchoscopy shows the level and whether the obstruction is within the airway or external; CT neck and thorax maps the lesion and the patency of the distal airway; a flow–volume loop shows the pattern of obstruction. Manage Temporary measures: sit up; heliox (its lower gas density improves flow past a fixed narrowing); high-flow humidified O₂; high-dose corticosteroid for oedema; nebulised adrenaline. Definitive treatment is usually by rigid bronchoscopy: mechanical debulking, laser or cryotherapy for tumour within the lumen; a self-expanding or silicone stent for external compression. Flexible bronchoscopy is for adjunctive procedures only. Afterwards: external-beam radiotherapy (or endobronchial brachytherapy) for radiosensitive tumour once the airway is secure; systemic therapy for chemosensitive disease. Securing the airway: inhalational or awake technique with the interventionalist and rigid bronchoscope in the room. Avoid routine paralysis or lying the patient flat, which can cause complete obstruction. Disposition & escalation Imminent arrest: theatre or bronchoscopy suite with thoracic surgery or ENT and anaesthesia; HDU or ICU afterwards. Central airway obstruction usually means advanced disease; agree a ceiling of care early, before deterioration. Pitfalls Sedation, muscle relaxant, or lying the patient flat before the airway is controlled. Calling the stridor asthma or COPD and giving bronchodilators alone. Waiting for imaging in a deteriorating patient instead of calling the interventional team. CHEST expert panel, Management of Central Airway Obstruction , Chest 2024 · Mudambi et al, J Thorac Dis 2017 (overview of malignant CAO). ESMO Handbook ch. 13 (Dyspnoea and Respiratory Failure).

records.title: Malignant bowel obstruction
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Mechanical or functional obstruction from intra-abdominal or peritoneal malignancy (commonly ovarian or colorectal). Colicky pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation. Nil by mouth, wide-bore NG tube on free drainage, IV crystalloid; correct hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia. Analgesia (opioid) and an antiemetic (haloperidol). Stop prokinetics if there is colic or complete obstruction. Antisecretory: hyoscine butylbromide 60–120 mg/24 h CSCI, or octreotide 300–600 µg/24 h SC or CSCI. Dexamethasone 6–16 mg/day IV (may speed resolution); early joint review by surgery and oncology. Recognise Colicky or constant abdominal pain, vomiting (faeculent when the obstruction is distal), distension, absolute constipation. Distinguish mechanical obstruction from functional causes (opioids, hypokalaemia), and obstruction at one level from obstruction at several; this decides whether surgery or a stent can help. Confirm Examine for localised tenderness or peritonism (strangulation or perforation). FBC, U&E; correct potassium and sodium. Erect chest and abdominal films, then CT abdomen and pelvis to show the level and cause, whether there is one level or several, and whether surgery, a stent or medical treatment is appropriate. Manage Decompression and resuscitation: nil by mouth, NG tube on free drainage, IV crystalloid, correct electrolytes. Symptom control by CSCI: analgesia (morphine or diamorphine); antiemetic (haloperidol first-line, or cyclizine or levomepromazine); antisecretory (hyoscine butylbromide 60–120 mg/24 h or octreotide 300–600 µg/24 h, up to about 800 µg); corticosteroid (dexamethasone 6–16 mg/day IV, which may lead to resolution). Metoclopramide only in incomplete obstruction without colic. Prokinetics worsen colic and are contraindicated in complete obstruction. Definitive treatment: surgery (bypass, resection or stoma) for fit patients with a single correctable mechanical level; a self-expanding metal stent for obstructing left-colon or gastroduodenal lesions; medical treatment alone where surgery is not appropriate (diffuse peritoneal disease, poor performance status). Disposition & escalation Joint decision by surgery, oncology and palliative care; prognosis matters as much as technique. Venting gastrostomy for refractory vomiting when a long-term NG tube is unacceptable. Pitfalls Missing strangulation or perforation (fever, peritonism, rising lactate) in a patient labelled as inoperable obstruction. Prokinetics in complete obstruction or colic. Deciding on medical treatment alone without a CT; a single reversible level may be treatable by surgery or a stent. MASCC evidence-based recommendations, medical management of MBO (2021 update), Support Care Cancer · Feuer & Broadley, Cochrane 2000 (corticosteroids, CD001219) · Ripamonti et al, Support Care Cancer 2000 (hyoscine butylbromide) · Mercadante octreotide RCTs. ESMO Handbook ch. 16 (Obstructive Bowel Disease).

records.title: Obstructive uropathy & urological emergencies
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Malignant ureteric obstruction from pelvic or retroperitoneal tumour or nodes, causing AKI, anuria and hyperkalaemia; or haemorrhagic cystitis with clot retention. Bilateral obstruction with AKI, anuria or urosepsis: urgent decompression by percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent. Do not wait. Check U&E and potassium; treat hyperkalaemia immediately. Haemorrhagic cystitis: 3-way catheter with continuous bladder irrigation; evacuate clots. Mesna is prophylaxis, not treatment. Renal-tract ultrasound (hydronephrosis), with or without CT; involve urology now; expect post-obstructive diuresis after relief. Recognise Obstructive uropathy: bilateral ureteric obstruction, or obstruction of a single functioning kidney, from pelvic or retroperitoneal tumour or nodal disease. Causes AKI and anuria; hyperkalaemia and uraemia are the causes of death. Haemorrhagic cystitis: visible haematuria or clot retention after cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide (acrolein toxicity), pelvic radiotherapy, or BK virus or adenovirus in immunosuppressed patients. Confirm U&E, potassium, venous gas. Renal-tract ultrasound for hydronephrosis, with or without non-contrast CT for level and cause. Catheterise for retention or clot. If bleeding: FBC, coagulation, group and save. Manage Decompression: percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent. Nephrostomy is often preferred in malignant obstruction because technical success is higher; a stent where feasible. Treat hyperkalaemia and uraemic complications at the same time; dialysis if refractory. Haemorrhagic cystitis: 3-way catheter with continuous bladder irrigation, manual or cystoscopic clot evacuation. Prophylaxis for ifosfamide (and high-dose cyclophosphamide) is hyperhydration plus mesna, in total 60–100% of the oxazaphosphorine dose, for example 20% IV at 0, 4 and 8 h. For refractory bleeding: intravesical agents, cystoscopic diathermy, or arterial embolisation. Post-obstructive diuresis: after relief of bilateral obstruction, monitor urine output and replace fluid and electrolytes; losses can be very large. Disposition & escalation Urology and nephrology. In advanced disease, consider whether decompression fits the goals of care; before a nephrostomy in end-stage malignant obstruction, discuss frankly with the patient what it can achieve. Pitfalls Discharging an anuric patient with bilateral obstruction; hyperkalaemia can be rapidly fatal. Giving mesna as treatment for established cystitis; it is prophylaxis only. Replacing too little fluid during post-obstructive diuresis. ESMO Handbook ch. 9 (Renal Failure and Urological Emergencies) · ASCO chemotherapy uroprotectant guideline (Hensley et al, JCO 2009) for mesna dosing · urological-emergency reviews.

records.title: Tumour lysis syndrome
records.subtitle: Metabolic
records.body: Rapid breakdown of a large number of tumour cells causing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hypocalcaemia, with or without AKI; occurs around treatment of bulky or rapidly proliferating disease. Isotonic IV fluids at a high rate (about 2500–3000 mL/m²/day; target urine output ≥2 mL/kg/h). Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV for high-risk or established TLS. Do not give if G6PD-deficient. Continuous cardiac monitoring; treat hyperkalaemia immediately. Bloods every 4–6 h (urate, K, PO₄, Ca, creatinine, LDH); involve nephrology early. Recognise Cairo–Bishop criteria. Laboratory TLS: 2 or more of the following, from 3 days before to 7 days after treatment: uric acid ≥476 µmol/L (8 mg/dL); K⁺ ≥6.0 mmol/L; phosphate ≥1.45 mmol/L (adults); corrected Ca²⁺ ≤1.75 mmol/L. Clinical TLS: laboratory TLS plus one of AKI (creatinine ≥1.5×ULN), cardiac arrhythmia or sudden death, or seizure. Howard (2011) changes: the two abnormalities must be present at the same time; the original criterion of a 25% change from baseline is dropped (rarely meaningful unless the value is already out of range); any symptomatic hypocalcaemia counts as clinical TLS. Highest risk: Burkitt or lymphoblastic lymphoma, ALL and AML with a high WBC, bulky chemosensitive tumours; higher still with existing renal impairment, volume depletion, or high LDH or urate. Confirm Urate, K, phosphate, corrected calcium, creatinine, LDH; ECG or telemetry; urine output. How often to check: high risk every 4–6 h; intermediate every 8–12 h; low risk daily, through the period of risk (depends on the regimen). Manage Prophylaxis by risk: low, allopurinol 300 mg/day and hydration; intermediate, allopurinol and hydration (rasburicase if urate rises); high or established, rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV daily and high-rate hydration. Do not combine allopurinol with rasburicase; allopurinol removes the substrate rasburicase acts on. Fluids: isotonic hyperhydration about 2500–3000 mL/m²/day (highest risk), target urine output ≥2 mL/kg/h. Avoid routine urinary alkalinisation; it increases calcium phosphate precipitation, especially when rasburicase is available. Loop diuretic if urine output stays low despite adequate hydration. Hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate to protect the heart, insulin–dextrose, salbutamol, binders; dialysis if refractory. Hyperphosphataemia: phosphate binders. Hypocalcaemia: treat only if symptomatic; calcium given when phosphate is high risks calcium phosphate deposition in tissues. Grade There is no graded severity scale. Cairo–Bishop separates laboratory from clinical TLS (clinical means organ involvement); Howard 2011 gives a clinical grade from 0 to IV. Disposition & escalation High-risk patients: monitored bed or HDU. Renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe hyperphosphataemia or symptomatic hypocalcaemia, fluid overload, or oliguric AKI; involve nephrology or ICU, with lower thresholds than for other AKI. Where possible, control urate before cytoreduction in very-high-risk disease. Pitfalls Rasburicase in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis, methaemoglobinaemia); screen patients of high-risk ancestry first. After rasburicase, send uric acid samples on ice; otherwise urate breaks down in the tube and the result is falsely low. Excess alkalinisation. Treating asymptomatic hypocalcaemia. Cairo & Bishop, Br J Haematol 2004 · Coiffier et al, JCO 2008 (TLS expert panel) · Howard et al, NEJM 2011 · British Society for Haematology (Jones et al) 2015 · NCCN. ESMO Handbook ch. 11.

records.title: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
records.subtitle: Metabolic
records.body: The most common life-threatening metabolic emergency in cancer, usually from PTHrP (humoral) or osteolysis. Dehydration, confusion, constipation, polyuria, AKI. Judge severity by the corrected calcium and the symptoms together. Confirm on corrected calcium (or ionised Ca); ECG (short QT, bradyarrhythmia). Rehydrate first: 0.9% saline IV ~200–500 mL/h, adjusted to volume status. Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over ≥15 min once rehydrated (reduce/withhold in renal impairment; denosumab if bisphosphonate-refractory or CrCl <30). Calcitonin 4 units/kg SC/IM q12h for rapid short-term lowering while the bisphosphonate takes effect. Recognise Suspect in any patient with cancer and new confusion, dehydration, constipation, polyuria or polydipsia, or AKI. Symptoms depend on how fast the calcium rises as well as on the level. Severity (corrected Ca): mild <3.0 mmol/L; moderate 3.0–3.4; severe >3.4 mmol/L (or symptomatic at any level). Severe or symptomatic hypercalcaemia is the emergency. Mechanism determines treatment: humoral (PTHrP, most solid tumours); osteolytic (myeloma, breast); 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin-D-mediated (lymphoma, granulomatous disease), which responds to steroids. Confirm Corrected calcium = measured total Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L); use ionised calcium when albumin or acid–base status is abnormal. PTH (suppressed in malignancy, which distinguishes it from primary hyperparathyroidism), PTHrP, phosphate, magnesium, renal function, ECG. Add 25-OH and 1,25-OH vitamin D if the cause is unclear (lymphoma or granuloma). Manage Rehydrate first: 0.9% saline ~200–500 mL/h adjusted to volume status (commonly 3–4 L over 24 h); this restores GFR and increases calcium excretion. Watch for fluid overload in cardiac or renal disease. Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over ≥15 min once volume-replete; nadir at day 4–7, effect lasts weeks. CrCl 30–60 mL/min: reduce to 3 mg; avoid if CrCl <30. Keep the patient hydrated to limit nephrotoxicity. Denosumab 120 mg SC (repeat on day 8 and day 15, then monthly) for hypercalcaemia refractory to bisphosphonate, or when renal impairment contraindicates a bisphosphonate. No renal dose adjustment, but watch for delayed and sometimes severe hypocalcaemia. Calcitonin 4–8 units/kg SC/IM every 6–12 h for the first 24–48 h. It acts within hours and gives a modest fall (~0.3–0.5 mmol/L) until the antiresorptive takes effect; tachyphylaxis by 48–72 h. Loop diuretics only for fluid overload after rehydration. They do not lower calcium and are harmful in a volume-depleted patient. Glucocorticoids (for example prednisolone 40–60 mg/day) for calcitriol-mediated hypercalcaemia of lymphoma or granulomatous disease. Dialysis for severe hypercalcaemia with renal failure or refractory to the above. Treat the cancer; lasting control needs effective anticancer treatment. Disposition & escalation Severe (>3.4 mmol/L) or symptomatic: monitored bed with telemetry and serial calcium and renal function. Nephrology for renal replacement in refractory disease or established renal failure. Recurrent hypercalcaemia means uncontrolled disease; involve the treating oncology team again. Pitfalls Giving a bisphosphonate before rehydrating; this adds to nephrotoxicity. Giving a loop diuretic first-line; it worsens the dehydration that raises the calcium. Reading an uncorrected calcium in a patient with low albumin (falsely reassuring). Missing delayed hypocalcaemia after denosumab; check calcium and correct vitamin D and magnesium. Asonitis et al / current UK practice review, Clin Med 2023 (PMID 37775175) · zoledronic acid prescribing information (renal thresholds) · ESMO Handbook ch. 10.

records.title: Hyponatraemia / SIADH
records.subtitle: Metabolic
records.body: The most common electrolyte disturbance in cancer; SIADH (SCLC, CNS disease, chemotherapy) is the usual euvolaemic cause. Risk depends on the rate of fall and the symptoms; correcting too fast causes the main harm. Grade the symptoms (seizures, obtundation or vomiting = severe) and assess volume status. Severe symptoms: 150 mL 3% hypertonic saline IV over 20 min, recheck Na, repeat 1–2 times until symptoms settle or Na has risen 5 mmol/L. Limit the rise to ≤10 mmol/L in 24 h and ≤18 mmol/L in 48 h (≤8 mmol/L in 24 h if demyelination risk is high). Over-correction causes osmotic demyelination. SIADH: fluid restriction and treatment of the cause. Send paired serum and urine osmolality and urine sodium before any treatment. Recognise Symptom severity sets the urgency. Severe: seizures, coma or fall in GCS, vomiting, cardiorespiratory distress. Moderate: nausea, confusion, headache. Mild: subtle or none. Symptoms depend on how fast the sodium fell as well as how low it is. SIADH, Bartter–Schwartz criteria: clinical euvolaemia, serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, urine sodium >30 mmol/L (on normal salt and water intake), no diuretic, and normal thyroid and adrenal function. Causes in cancer: ectopic ADH (SCLC and others), CNS metastases, drugs (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, platinum), nausea, pain, opioids. Confirm Paired serum and urine osmolality and urine sodium; glucose (to exclude translocational hyponatraemia and pseudohyponatraemia); TFTs and 9 am cortisol (hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency mimic SIADH); careful volume assessment to separate hypovolaemic, euvolaemic and hypervolaemic causes. Manage Severe or symptomatic (any sodium level): 150 mL 3% saline over 20 min (about 2 mL/kg), recheck sodium, repeat until symptoms improve or sodium has risen 5 mmol/L. Target a rise of 5 mmol/L in the first hour to relieve cerebral oedema, then stop the hypertonic saline and stay within the daily limit. Correction limits: ≤10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and ≤18 mmol/L in the first 48 h. Aim for ≤8 mmol/L in 24 h where demyelination risk is high (sodium <105 mmol/L, hypokalaemia, alcohol-use disorder, malnutrition, advanced liver disease). If the limit is exceeded, lower the sodium again with 5% dextrose, with or without desmopressin. Chronic SIADH: fluid restriction to <800–1000 mL/day first line; if not enough, add oral urea, or tolvaptan (a vasopressin-receptor antagonist) with caution. Vaptans can correct too fast and are hepatotoxic; avoid in liver disease and do not use beyond 30 days. Treat the cause: systemic therapy for SCLC; stop the causative drug. Disposition & escalation Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia: HDU or monitored bed, with sodium checked every 2–4 h during active correction. Involve endocrinology or nephrology for refractory SIADH, diagnostic uncertainty, or over-correction that needs active lowering. Pitfalls Correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly; osmotic demyelination does more harm than the low sodium. Starting a vaptan during fluid restriction, or in liver disease. Diagnosing SIADH without excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. Treating the number rather than the patient; asymptomatic chronic hyponatraemia at 125 mmol/L does not need hypertonic saline. Related: brain or leptomeningeal disease may contribute; see raised ICP (this module). Spasovski et al, European clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia, Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47 (PMID 24569125) · Verbalis et al, US expert-panel recommendations, Am J Med 2013 (PMID 24074529; high-risk ≤8 mmol/L target) · ESMO Handbook ch. 12.

records.title: Febrile neutropaenia & septic shock
records.subtitle: Infective
records.body: Fever in a neutropenic patient is a medical emergency. Treat as sepsis until proven otherwise; manage as septic shock as soon as hypotension or hypoperfusion appears. Empirical antipseudomonal β-lactam within 1 hour: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV, cefepime 2 g IV, or meropenem 1–2 g IV. Do not wait for the count or cultures. Take blood cultures (peripheral and every central lumen), lactate, FBC and renal and liver tests first if this causes no delay; the antibiotic is not held for them. If hypotensive or lactate ≥2 mmol/L: Surviving Sepsis bundle; ≥30 mL/kg crystalloid over 3 h, norepinephrine to MAP ≥65 mmHg, source control. Add vancomycin only for a specific indication (see Manage); not routinely. Recognise Neutropenia: ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L, or <1.0 ×10⁹/L and expected to fall below 0.5 within 48 h. Fever: a single oral temperature ≥38.3 °C, or ≥38.0 °C sustained over 1 h. A single fever is enough to start treatment; often there is no localising sign and no source. Highest risk: ANC <0.1 ×10⁹/L, expected neutropenia >7 days, haematological malignancy or HSCT. Signs of progression to septic shock: hypotension, lactate ≥2 mmol/L, mottling, new confusion. Confirm Blood cultures from a peripheral vein and from each central lumen; FBC, renal and liver tests, lactate; urinalysis, CXR and swabs from sites suggested by symptoms. Do not delay the antibiotic for these tests. Risk stratification (MASCC index). Score ≥21: low risk of complications, suitable for the oral or outpatient pathway. Score <21: high risk; admit for IV therapy. The index scores burden of illness, no hypotension, no COPD, solid tumour or no previous fungal infection, no dehydration, onset as an outpatient, and age <60. Manage First dose within 1 h. Antipseudomonal β-lactam alone: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 h, cefepime 2 g IV every 8 h, or meropenem 1–2 g IV every 8 h, adjusted to renal function. Carbapenem first line if a resistant organism is likely. Vancomycin only for a specific indication: haemodynamic instability or severe sepsis, suspected catheter-related infection, skin or soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, known MRSA colonisation, or Gram-positive cocci in blood before identification. Stop at 48–72 h if not confirmed. Low risk (MASCC ≥21), stable and taking oral medicines: oral ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin-clavulanate, with a set pathway for review and readmission. Not if the patient was taking fluoroquinolone prophylaxis. Septic shock: Surviving Sepsis bundle; ≥30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid over 3 h, norepinephrine first line to MAP ≥65 mmHg, repeat lactate, remove an infected line. Widen cover for resistant organisms and add antifungal cover if not improving. G-CSF is not routine treatment for established FN; its use by risk is as prophylaxis (see Tox). Disposition & escalation High risk (MASCC <21): admit for IV antibiotics; profound or prolonged neutropenia: monitored bed. Shock, rising lactate or organ dysfunction: ICU. Reassess at 48–72 h: narrow treatment on culture results; continue until afebrile with a recovering ANC. Involve infectious diseases and haematology early. Pitfalls Delaying the first dose for cultures, imaging or line access; start within the hour. Giving vancomycin to every patient; keep it for a specific indication and stop if not confirmed. Missing developing shock in a febrile patient who looks stable; recheck lactate and perfusion. Applying MASCC to a patient who is already unstable; the index assumes an uncomplicated presentation. Related: G-CSF prophylaxis (primary and secondary) and FN risk by chemotherapy regimen are in Tox; this card covers the acute episode. Definition, empiric therapy and vancomycin indications: Freifeld AG et al, IDSA clinical practice guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2011;52:e56–e93 (PMID 21205990). Low-risk / outpatient oral pathway: Taplitz RA et al, ASCO–IDSA guideline, J Clin Oncol 2018;36:1443–1453 (PMID 29461916). MASCC index: Klastersky J et al, J Clin Oncol 2000;18:3038–3051 (PMID 10944139). Septic shock: Evans L et al, Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021, Intensive Care Med 2021;47:1181–1247 (PMID 34599691). ESMO Handbook ch. 21.

records.title: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis)
records.subtitle: Infective
records.body: Fever, abdominal pain (often right lower quadrant) and diarrhoea in a neutropenic patient; inflammation and necrosis of the caecum and bowel wall. High mortality if missed. Broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic and antipseudomonal Gram-negative cover: piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (or cefepime plus metronidazole). Bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and electrolyte correction. Urgent CT abdomen and pelvis; repeated abdominal examination; early surgical review. No antimotility or antidiarrhoeal drugs. Recognise Fever, abdominal pain (classically right lower quadrant, over the caecum) and diarrhoea during neutropenia, typically 1–2 weeks after cytotoxic chemotherapy (high-dose cytarabine, taxanes, intensive induction). Distension, rebound, peritonism or GI bleeding suggest transmural necrosis and impending perforation. Confirm CT abdomen and pelvis is the test of choice: circumferential bowel-wall thickening (caecum, with or without ascending colon), mural oedema, pericolic fat stranding, with or without pneumatosis. FBC, lactate, coagulation and blood cultures; stool for Clostridioides difficile, the main differential. Avoid colonoscopy; risk of perforation in inflamed neutropenic bowel. Manage Antibiotics with anaerobic cover: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 h or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 h; with cefepime, add metronidazole. Add antifungal cover if not improving or neutropenia persists. Supportive care: bowel rest, nasogastric tube for ileus or obstruction, IV fluids, correction of electrolytes and coagulopathy, transfusion to target. Neutrophil recovery determines outcome; G-CSF is often used to shorten neutropenia. Avoid antimotility drugs (loperamide, opioids); they cause stasis and toxin retention and increase the risk of perforation. Disposition & escalation Admit to a monitored bed with repeated examination and imaging. Involve surgeons early but operate selectively: surgery is for perforation, uncontrolled GI bleeding, or deterioration or suspected necrosis despite full medical treatment. Most cases resolve with neutrophil recovery and conservative care; ICU for haemodynamic instability. Pitfalls Missing the diagnosis; neutropenia reduces abdominal signs, so keep a low threshold for CT. Leaving out anaerobic cover. Antimotility drugs, or early colonoscopy. Not excluding C. difficile. Gorschlüter M et al, systematic analysis of neutropenic enterocolitis in adults, Eur J Haematol 2005 (PMID 16504141); Nesher L & Rolston KV, Clin Infect Dis 2013;56:711 (review); current practice syntheses (StatPearls, Medscape). Antibiotic backbone aligns with the IDSA febrile-neutropenia guideline (Freifeld 2011, PMID 21205990). ESMO Handbook ch. 19.

records.title: Acute transfusion reactions
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Any new fever, hypotension, dyspnoea, rash or pain during or shortly after a transfusion. The dangerous reactions (ABO haemolysis, bacterial sepsis, anaphylaxis, TRALI) start early and at onset can look the same as a benign febrile reaction. Stop the transfusion; keep the line open with 0.9% saline. Recheck patient identity against the unit and the compatibility label; ABO incompatibility is a bedside identification error. ABC and observations; treat by presentation: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg for anaphylaxis, fluids with or without vasopressors for hypotension, O₂ for hypoxia. Return the unit and giving set to the laboratory; send FBC, repeat group and crossmatch, DAT, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, coagulation, and blood cultures (patient and unit). Recognise: acute reactions Acute haemolytic (ABO incompatibility): fever, loin or infusion-site pain, hypotension, dark urine, DIC, oliguria, within minutes of starting. A medical emergency. Febrile non-haemolytic (FNHTR): fever alone, with or without rigors, haemodynamically stable. A diagnosis of exclusion. Allergic and anaphylactic: urticaria or pruritus (mild), progressing to bronchospasm, angio-oedema and hypotension (severe; consider IgA deficiency). TACO and TRALI (both cause dyspnoea and hypoxia within about 6 h). TACO is circulatory overload: hypertension, raised JVP, positive fluid balance, responds to diuretics; risk in elderly patients and in cardiac or renal disease. TRALI is non-cardiogenic: hypotension, fever, normal JVP, bilateral infiltrates, no response to diuretics; respiratory support and notify the blood service. Bacterial contamination (septic reaction): rapid high fever, rigors, hypotension, collapse; most often with platelets (stored at room temperature). Confirm Bedside identity check first. Haemolysis: DAT, repeat crossmatch, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, free haemoglobin, urinalysis. Sepsis: paired blood cultures (patient and unit) and Gram stain of the unit. Respiratory: CXR to separate TACO from TRALI; raised BNP and positive fluid balance favour TACO. Manage by type Mild febrile: paracetamol; slow the transfusion and observe closely, or restart with caution if the fever settles and there are no other features. Mild allergic (urticaria only): antihistamine; may restart slowly under observation. Anaphylaxis: stop permanently; IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (500 µg), repeated every 5 min as needed; O₂, IV fluids, antihistamine or steroid as adjuncts. Use washed or IgA-deficient components in future. Acute haemolytic: stop; IV fluids at a high rate to maintain urine output; support for DIC and AKI. Treat as an ABO error until proven otherwise and inform the laboratory and haematology. TACO: stop or slow; sit the patient up, O₂, IV furosemide. If transfusion is still needed, restart at a lower rate with diuretic cover. TRALI: stop; respiratory support (may need ventilation) and supportive care. Do not give diuretics. Notify the blood service (implicated donor). Septic: stop; cultures (patient and unit), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, resuscitation; return the unit for Gram stain and culture. Disposition & escalation Haemodynamic or respiratory compromise: ICU. Notify the hospital transfusion laboratory and team early, and report serious reactions to the national haemovigilance scheme (for example SHOT and SABRE in the UK). Do not issue further components for that patient until the cause is known. Pitfalls Not stopping for a fever alone; early ABO haemolysis and bacterial sepsis cannot be told apart from a benign febrile reaction at onset. Giving diuretics in TRALI (it is not volume overload). Skipping the bedside identity check, the cause of most fatal ABO errors. Discarding the unit before it can be cultured and Gram-stained. Related: DIC (this module) may complicate acute haemolytic reactions; febrile neutropenia (this module) overlaps the septic differential. Tinegate et al, BCSH/BSH guideline on the investigation and management of acute transfusion reactions, Br J Haematol 2013;159:143–153 (PMID 22928769) · ESMO Handbook ch. 22.

records.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Consumptive coagulopathy caused by an underlying trigger (sepsis, APL or other malignancy, obstetric emergency, trauma), with microvascular thrombosis and bleeding at the same time. Treatment of DIC is treatment of the trigger. Identify and treat the trigger now: sepsis (source control and antibiotics), APL, solid tumour. This is the only definitive treatment. Send a DIC screen: platelets, PT and APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer or FDP. Repeat it regularly; DIC changes over hours. Score with the ISTH overt-DIC criteria (≥5 = overt DIC). Give blood products according to bleeding and the trend, not laboratory values alone. Recognise Bleeding (oozing from cannula sites or wounds, mucosal bleeding, ecchymoses) or thrombosis, or both, with organ dysfunction. Suspect in septic shock, acute promyelocytic leukaemia and other acute leukaemias, and metastatic mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma. Chronic compensated DIC (solid tumours) often presents with thrombosis (Trousseau syndrome) rather than bleeding. Confirm: ISTH overt-DIC score Use only when there is an underlying disorder known to cause DIC. Platelets >100 = 0 · 50–100 = 1 · <50 = 2 Fibrin marker (D-dimer or FDP): no rise = 0 · moderate = 2 · strong = 3 PT prolongation <3 s = 0 · 3–6 s = 1 · >6 s = 2 Fibrinogen >1 g/L = 0 · <1 g/L = 1 ≥5 = overt DIC (repeat the score daily); <5 suggests non-overt DIC; repeat in 1–2 days. The score supports the diagnosis; it does not replace the clinical picture or the serial trend. Manage Treat the trigger: antibiotics and source control for sepsis; start ATRA immediately for suspected APL. Nothing else reverses DIC. Blood products only for bleeding, high bleeding risk, or before a procedure: Platelets if bleeding and <50 × 10⁹/L, or not bleeding and <20 × 10⁹/L. FFP if bleeding with PT or APTT >1.5 × normal. Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen stays <1.5 g/L despite FFP. Heparin: prophylactic-dose LMWH for VTE prophylaxis in DIC without bleeding; therapeutic anticoagulation only where thrombosis predominates (Trousseau syndrome, purpura fulminans). Not routine, and not during bleeding. Do not correct laboratory values in a stable patient who is not bleeding. Disposition & escalation Haemodynamic instability or major bleeding: ICU. Involve haematology urgently; suspected APL needs immediate haematology referral the same day. Pitfalls APL with DIC: start ATRA on clinical suspicion, before genetic confirmation, and give full coagulation support (platelets >30–50 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen >1.5 g/L). Early death in APL is mainly from the coagulopathy, not leukostasis; avoid invasive procedures that are not needed. Transfusing to a laboratory target in a patient who is not bleeding. Missing APL as the cause of coagulopathy in a new acute leukaemia. Withholding VTE prophylaxis in DIC without bleeding. Expecting the values to correct before the trigger is controlled; they do not. Related: febrile neutropenia and septic shock (this module), the most common trigger of DIC; acute haemolytic transfusion reactions (this module) can also cause DIC. Levi et al, BCSH guideline on the diagnosis and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation, Br J Haematol 2009;145:24–33 (PMID 19222477) · Taylor et al, ISTH/SSC overt-DIC scoring system, Thromb Haemost 2001;86:1327–1330 (PMID 11816725) · ESMO Handbook ch. 22.

records.title: Hyperviscosity syndrome / leukostasis
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Two emergencies of impaired blood flow: paraprotein hyperviscosity (Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or myeloma) and leukostasis (acute leukaemia with a very high blast count). Both cause visual, neurological and mucosal or respiratory symptoms; both need urgent reduction of the paraprotein or the blast count. Paraprotein hyperviscosity: urgent plasma exchange and treatment of the underlying clone. If symptomatic, do not wait for a viscosity result. Leukostasis: urgent cytoreduction with hydroxyurea or leukapheresis, or both, then induction chemotherapy; start TLS prophylaxis (hydration plus rasburicase or allopurinol). Avoid red cell transfusion until cytoreduced; added red cells raise viscosity and can worsen occlusion. Correct thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy. Fundoscopy, neurological and respiratory assessment; senior haematology review now. Recognise Paraprotein hyperviscosity: high circulating monoclonal protein, usually IgM in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia (also IgA or IgG myeloma). Classic triad: mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding), visual disturbance (retinopathy with dilated, segmented retinal veins and haemorrhages), and neurological signs (headache, vertigo, confusion, coma). Symptoms are usual once serum viscosity exceeds about 4 cP, although the threshold varies between patients. Leukostasis: symptomatic occlusion of small vessels by leukaemic blasts, typically AML with WBC >100 ×10⁹/L (some series report risk from about 50–75; ALL and chronic leukaemias tolerate much higher counts). Presents with hypoxia or dyspnoea and pulmonary infiltrates, and neurological signs (confusion, visual change, headache); fever is common. Hyperleukocytosis is the laboratory finding; leukostasis is the clinical syndrome. Confirm Hyperviscosity: serum viscosity, immunoglobulins and paraprotein quantification, serum protein electrophoresis; fundoscopy; FBC, renal function, calcium. Treat on clinical grounds; do not wait for viscosity if the patient is symptomatic. Leukostasis: FBC and blast count, film, coagulation and fibrinogen (to exclude DIC, especially in APL), LDH, urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium and creatinine (TLS), ABG and CXR. The diagnosis is clinical; normal imaging does not exclude it. Manage Paraprotein hyperviscosity: urgent therapeutic plasma exchange removes the paraprotein and relieves symptoms while definitive treatment starts. IgM is mostly intravascular, so a modest fall in concentration lowers viscosity substantially. Follow at once with treatment of the clone; repeat exchange according to symptoms. Leukostasis: urgent cytoreduction. Hydroxyurea can start before the leukaemia subtype is confirmed. Leukapheresis lowers the count rapidly in symptomatic hyperleukocytosis (an adjunct, with no proven survival benefit) and is avoided in acute promyelocytic leukaemia (it worsens the coagulopathy). Definitive control is prompt induction chemotherapy. TLS prophylaxis for leukostasis: IV hydration plus rasburicase (high risk) or allopurinol, with close electrolyte monitoring. Transfusion: withhold red cells until the count or paraprotein is reduced, unless anaemia is critical; platelets and FFP as needed for bleeding or coagulopathy. Disposition & escalation Both are haematological emergencies needing a monitored bed and immediate haematology involvement; arrange apheresis (plasma exchange or leukapheresis) urgently. ICU for respiratory failure or reduced consciousness. Early mortality in leukostasis is high; cytoreduction and induction must not be delayed. Pitfalls Transfusing red cells before the paraprotein or white count is reduced. Waiting for a viscosity result before plasma exchange in a symptomatic patient. Forgetting TLS prophylaxis when reducing a high blast count. Leukapheresis in APL; it worsens the coagulopathy. Give ATRA and coagulation support first. Related: TLS (this module, Metabolic). Leukostasis and its treatment can cause tumour lysis; give TLS prophylaxis at the same time. Leukostasis / hyperleukocytosis: Röllig C & Ehninger G, 'How I treat hyperleukocytosis in acute myeloid leukemia,' Blood 2015;125:3246–3252 (PMID 25778528). Paraprotein hyperviscosity: Gertz MA et al, hyperviscosity in paraprotein-secreting conditions, Front Oncol 2020;10:815 (PMC7248405). ESMO Handbook ch. 22–23 (haematological emergencies).

records.title: Major haemorrhage (incl. massive haemoptysis)
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Uncontrolled or life-threatening bleeding: resuscitate, activate the major-haemorrhage protocol, reverse anticoagulation and achieve definitive source control. In massive haemoptysis, asphyxiation causes death before blood loss does. ABC: protect the airway, high-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch; activate the major-haemorrhage protocol. Transfuse in a fixed ratio (about 1:1:1 red cells, FFP, platelets) until laboratory results guide replacement; give calcium; keep the patient warm; limit crystalloid. Reverse anticoagulation by agent (see Manage); tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h, in trauma, surgical or obstetric bleeding. Definitive source control (surgery, interventional radiology or endoscopy) without delay. Recognise Haemorrhage that threatens life by volume or by site: haemodynamic instability, continuing visible loss, or bleeding into a critical space (airway, cranium, pericardium). In patients with cancer, suspect tumour erosion of a vessel, thrombocytopenia, DIC or anticoagulant effect. Massive haemoptysis (large volume, or any volume that impairs gas exchange) is first an airway emergency; a small amount of blood can fill the airways and cause asphyxiation. Confirm FBC, coagulation screen with fibrinogen, group and save or crossmatch, U&E, calcium, lactate and a blood gas; drug history for anticoagulants and antiplatelets, with time of last dose. Find the source by imaging or endoscopy as the patient's condition allows; for haemoptysis, CT angiography and bronchoscopy identify the bleeding side. Resuscitation and investigation run at the same time. Manage Resuscitation: major-haemorrhage protocol with fixed-ratio products (about 1:1:1), then laboratory-guided replacement (fibrinogen, platelets, coagulation) as results return; ionised calcium replacement; active warming; permissive hypotension until source control where appropriate. Reversal of anticoagulation by agent. Warfarin: IV vitamin K and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban): andexanet alfa, or 4-factor PCC where it is not available. Heparin: protamine. Platelets for a bleeding patient with thrombocytopenia or on antiplatelet treatment. Tranexamic acid: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h. Benefit is established in trauma (give within 3 h) and in surgical and obstetric haemorrhage. Not for GI bleeding (no mortality benefit, more VTE). Massive haemoptysis: protect the airway (early intubation if blood is filling the airway); position bleeding side down to protect the other lung; consider selective intubation of the non-bleeding lung; urgent bronchoscopy to localise and tamponade. Bronchial artery embolisation is first line for control; surgery if refractory. Source control is the priority throughout: surgery, IR embolisation or endoscopic therapy. Blood products support the patient until the source is controlled; they do not treat it. Disposition & escalation Call the resuscitation or major-haemorrhage team, the transfusion laboratory, and the relevant proceduralist (surgery, IR, endoscopy, thoracic surgery) at the same time. ICU or theatre for continuing instability. Monitor coagulation and calcium throughout resuscitation; correct hypothermia and acidosis, which sustain bleeding. Pitfalls Resuscitating with crystalloid instead of blood products; this dilutes clotting factors and worsens coagulopathy. Routine tranexamic acid in GI bleeding (HALT-IT: no benefit, more thrombosis). Missing the anticoagulant; always take the drug and last-dose history and give specific reversal. Treating massive haemoptysis as a lung problem before it is treated as an airway problem; secure the airway and position the patient first. Allowing hypothermia, acidosis and hypocalcaemia to develop during large-volume transfusion. Transfusion ratio: Holcomb JB et al, PROPPR, JAMA 2015;313:471–482 (PMID 25647203). Tranexamic acid in trauma: CRASH-2, Lancet 2010;376:23–32 (PMID 20554319); GI-bleed caveat: HALT-IT, Lancet 2020;395:1927–1936 (PMID 32563378). Anticoagulant reversal: ISTH SSC guidance, J Thromb Haemost 2024 (PMID 39029742) — idarucizumab (RE-VERSE AD, PMID 28693366) and andexanet alfa (ANNEXA-4, PMID 30730782). Massive haemoptysis: Davidson K & Shojaee S, 'Managing Massive Hemoptysis,' Chest 2020 (PMID 31374211). ESMO Handbook ch. 23 (bleeding) & ch. 15 (haemoptysis).

records.title: Acute cancer-associated VTE / pulmonary embolism
records.subtitle: Vascular
records.body: Cancer-associated DVT or PE. Risk of recurrence and risk of bleeding are both high; choice of agent depends on tumour site and bleeding risk. Anticoagulate: weight-based LMWH, or a DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, or edoxaban; edoxaban only after ≥5 days of LMWH). Haemodynamically unstable (high-risk) PE: systemic thrombolysis unless contraindicated; bleeding risk is higher in cancer. Before choosing an agent, consider a GI or GU primary and the bleeding risk; check platelets and renal function. For thrombocytopenia, dose-reduce or hold rather than stop. Recognise New dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, unilateral leg swelling, unexplained tachycardia, hypoxia or syncope in a patient with cancer. Incidental PE on staging CT is treated. High-risk (massive) PE = obstructive shock or hypotension. Confirm CTPA for PE, compression ultrasound for DVT. ECG, troponin and echo (RV strain) identify high-risk PE. FBC, renal function and baseline coagulation guide agent and dose. Manage Anticoagulate for at least 6 months while the cancer is active. Options: LMWH (for example dalteparin 200 IU/kg once daily for 1 month, then 150 IU/kg once daily): the long-standing standard, and preferred in luminal GI or GU cancer or high bleeding risk. Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily. CARAVAGGIO: recurrent VTE 5.6% vs 7.9% with dalteparin (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.37–1.07); major bleeding 3.8% vs 4.0% (HR 0.82; 0.40–1.69). Edoxaban 60 mg once daily after ≥5 days of LMWH. Hokusai-VTE Cancer: recurrent VTE or major bleeding 12.8% vs 13.5% (HR 0.97; 0.70–1.36); less recurrent VTE (7.9% vs 11.3%) but more major bleeding (6.9% vs 4.0%; risk difference 2.9 percentage points, 0.1–5.6), mostly upper GI bleeding in patients with GI cancer. Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks, then 20 mg once daily. SELECT-D: VTE recurrence at 6 months 4% vs 11% (HR 0.43; 0.19–0.99), but more clinically relevant non-major bleeding (13% vs 4%; HR 3.76; 1.63–8.69). High-risk (massive) PE: systemic thrombolysis for haemodynamic instability; catheter-directed therapy or embolectomy where thrombolysis is contraindicated. Cancer increases bleeding risk with any of these options. Thrombocytopenia: reduce or hold the dose rather than stop; guideline platelet thresholds are about 25–50 ×10⁹/L. Follow local protocol. Disposition & escalation High-risk PE: HDU or ICU on a thrombolysis pathway. Recurrent VTE on anticoagulation: increase the LMWH dose. Use an IVC filter only for a true, continuing contraindication to anticoagulation, and retrieve it when possible. Pitfalls DOACs in luminal GI or GU cancer: more GI and GU bleeding (Hokusai, SELECT-D); prefer apixaban or LMWH. Treating incidental PE as benign; recurrence risk is similar, so it is anticoagulated. Using an IVC filter instead of anticoagulation. Stopping anticoagulation for mild thrombocytopenia instead of adjusting the dose. Related: DIC and major haemorrhage (this module) for the bleeding patient who also needs anticoagulation. Agnelli et al, CARAVAGGIO , NEJM 2020;382:1599 · Raskob et al, Hokusai-VTE Cancer , NEJM 2018;378:615 · Young et al, SELECT-D , JCO 2018;36:2017 · Farge et al, ITAC 2022, Lancet Oncol 2022;23:e334 · Key et al, ASCO VTE guideline update, JCO 2020. ESMO Handbook ch. 2 (Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer Patients).

records.title: Cytokine release syndrome
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Excessive cytokine release after CAR-T or T-cell-engaging bispecific antibodies; fever with or without hypotension or hypoxia, usually within days of infusion. Recognise: fever ≥38 °C after immune-effector-cell therapy. Exclude and treat neutropenic sepsis at the same time. Grade by ASTCT (see below). Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg) for grade ≥2 (and persistent grade 1). Supportive care: fluids for hypotension, O₂; add dexamethasone for tocilizumab-refractory or grade ≥3 CRS; ICU for grade 3–4. Recognise Onset typically 1–14 days after CAR-T (often day 2–3); can be within hours with bispecifics. Fever is the defining feature, followed by hypotension or hypoxia, or both. Infection can mimic CRS or occur with it; screen and give cover. May occur with ICANS. Confirm Observations (temperature, BP, SpO₂), sepsis screen (cultures, lactate), FBC, renal and liver tests, CRP and ferritin (for the trend; not specific), coagulation (CRS can cause coagulopathy or HLH). Continuous monitoring. Grade: ASTCT 2019 G1 fever ≥38 °C (no hypotension, no hypoxia). G2 fever with hypotension not needing vasopressors, or hypoxia needing low-flow O₂ (≤6 L/min), or both. G3 fever with hypotension needing one vasopressor (with or without vasopressin), or hypoxia needing high-flow O₂ (>6 L/min), or both. G4 fever with hypotension needing more than one vasopressor (excluding vasopressin), or hypoxia needing positive-pressure ventilation, or both. Fever may settle after antipyretics or tocilizumab; grade on hypotension and hypoxia from then on. Manage by grade G1: supportive care, antipyretics, fluids; empirical antibiotics if neutropenic; tocilizumab if fever persists. G2: tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg), repeated every 8 h if needed (≤3 doses in 24 h, ≤4 in total); fluid boluses; O₂; add dexamethasone 10 mg IV if the response is inadequate. G3: tocilizumab and dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 h; vasopressor; ICU. G4: tocilizumab and high-dose methylprednisolone (1 g/day); ICU, more than one vasopressor or ventilation; anakinra or another anti-cytokine agent for refractory CRS. Disposition & escalation G1–2: monitored ward or HDU according to protocol; G3–4: ICU. Notify the cellular-therapy team and follow the product and institutional protocol. Watch for ICANS and for HLH or MAS. Pitfalls Missing neutropenic sepsis as a cause of the fever (treat both). Withholding tocilizumab in CRS with hypotension. Withholding steroids when indicated; at recommended doses they do not appear to reduce CAR-T efficacy. Using tocilizumab for ICANS; it penetrates the CNS poorly. Use steroids for ICANS. Related: ICANS (this module); steroid doses by grade overlap the immunotherapy toxicity guidance in Tox. Lee DW et al, ASTCT (ASBMT) consensus, Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 2019;25:625–638 · Santomasso et al, ASCO guideline, JCO 2021 · NCCN Management of Immunotherapy-Related Toxicities. records.title: Anaphylaxis, hypersensitivity & infusion reactions
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Acute reaction during or shortly after a systemic anticancer drug, from a mild infusion reaction to airway or circulatory collapse. Treat as anaphylaxis as soon as airway, breathing or circulation is threatened. Stop the infusion; keep IV access; call for help. Anaphylaxis: adrenaline 500 µg IM (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 min if no improvement. Airway and high-flow O₂; lie flat with legs raised (sit up if breathing is the main problem); IV crystalloid bolus for hypotension. Antihistamine and corticosteroid are adjuncts, given after adrenaline and never instead of it. Recognise Anaphylaxis = acute onset of a life-threatening airway problem (swelling, stridor, hoarseness), breathing problem (wheeze, hypoxia) or circulation problem (hypotension, collapse), usually with skin changes (urticaria, angio-oedema). Skin signs are absent in up to a fifth of cases, so their absence does not exclude it. The mechanism determines management of later cycles: Standard infusion-related reaction (monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab and cetuximab; often the first infusion): fever, chills, flushing, rigors, back pain, mild dyspnoea from cytokine release. Usually settles with stopping or slowing the infusion and premedication. Hypersensitivity: taxanes (often at the first exposure, a reaction to the Cremophor or polysorbate vehicle) and platinums. Platinum hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated and typically appears after several cycles (usually the 6th or later carboplatin exposure), once the patient is sensitised. Cetuximab reactions at first exposure can be IgE-mediated (anti-α-gal antibodies) and severe. Confirm The diagnosis is clinical; do not delay adrenaline for tests. Continuous monitoring (BP, SpO₂, ECG). Serial mast-cell tryptase (as soon as safe, at about 1–2 h, and a baseline at ≥24 h) supports a later diagnosis of anaphylaxis but does not guide acute treatment. Record the drug, cycle number and timing for the allergy and immunology referral. Manage Adrenaline is the only first-line drug: 500 µg IM (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 min until response. IV adrenaline (titrated, for example 50 µg boluses) is for refractory shock in a monitored setting, given by staff trained to use it; give IM first. Airway and breathing: high-flow O₂, nebulised salbutamol for bronchospasm, nebulised adrenaline for upper-airway oedema; call anaesthetics early for a threatened airway. Circulation: lie flat with legs raised; rapid IV crystalloid bolus (500–1000 mL, repeat as needed); for refractory hypotension, critical care for an adrenaline infusion with or without other vasopressors. Adjuncts (second line, after adrenaline): a non-sedating antihistamine and a corticosteroid. They treat the skin features and may reduce a biphasic reaction, but neither is life-saving and neither replaces adrenaline. Standard infusion reaction (not anaphylaxis): stop and treat symptoms; once settled, restart at a slower rate with premedication. Grade No single oncology scale guides acute treatment; any threat to airway, breathing or circulation starts the anaphylaxis pathway. Afterwards, infusion reactions are graded by CTCAE and hypersensitivity severity by the Ring and Messmer or Brown grades; these inform rechallenge planning, not resuscitation. Disposition & escalation After anaphylaxis, observe for a biphasic reaction: 6–12 h after a severe or refractory reaction, ≥2 h after one that resolved quickly. Monitored bed or HDU if adrenaline was repeated or shock occurred. Refer to allergy and immunology before the next cycle. Later cycles depend on the mechanism. Mild infusion reaction: premedicate and slow the rate. Confirmed IgE hypersensitivity to a drug that remains the best treatment (platinum, taxane): formal graded desensitisation in a monitored setting, not simple rechallenge. Desensitisation gives temporary tolerance only and must be repeated at each cycle. Pitfalls Giving antihistamine or steroid first and delaying adrenaline; the most common fatal error in anaphylaxis. Giving adrenaline IV or subcutaneously by default; IM into the thigh is the standard route. Sitting or standing a hypotensive patient; this can cause fatal circulatory collapse. Keep the patient flat. Managing true platinum hypersensitivity by slowing the rate; the reaction worsens on rechallenge and needs desensitisation. Resuscitation Council UK Guidelines for the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (Whitaker et al, Resuscitation 2021) · WAO anaphylaxis guidance · oncology hypersensitivity / desensitisation literature (Castells). ESMO Handbook ch. on hypersensitivity / infusion reactions.

records.title: Vesicant chemotherapy extravasation
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Leak of a vesicant from the vein into surrounding tissue: pain, swelling, burning or loss of blood return at the cannula. Anthracyclines and vinca alkaloids can cause progressive necrosis if managed wrongly. Stop the infusion immediately; leave the cannula in place for now. Disconnect and aspirate residual drug through the cannula, then remove it. Elevate the limb; mark and photograph the area; do not flush or apply pressure. Identify the drug. Anthracycline: cold pack and dexrazoxane. Vinca alkaloid: warm pack and hyaluronidase. Recognise Suspect extravasation with any burning or stinging pain, swelling, erythema, induration or loss of blood return during a vesicant infusion; symptoms may be subtle and can be hidden with a central line. Vesicants (tissue necrosis): anthracyclines (doxorubicin, epirubicin, daunorubicin), vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbine), and others (mitomycin C, dactinomycin, trabectedin). Irritants (inflammation without necrosis): platinums, taxanes, etoposide; lower risk, but still stop and assess. Confirm The diagnosis is clinical. Record the drug, estimated volume, cannula site and time; outline the affected area and photograph it for comparison over time. Early plastic or surgical review for a large-volume anthracycline extravasation or any blistering or necrosis. Manage All vesicants: stop, disconnect, aspirate residual drug through the cannula while it is still in place, then remove it; elevate; do not flush the line or apply direct pressure. Anthracyclines: cold and dexrazoxane. Intermittent cold packs (about 20 min, several times daily) cause vasoconstriction and keep the drug localised; do not use warmth. Dexrazoxane IV for significant extravasation: 1000 mg/m² on day 1, 1000 mg/m² on day 2, 500 mg/m² on day 3 (cap at BSA 2 m²; reduce by 50% if CrCl <40 mL/min). First dose within 6 h, then at the same time each day, into a different limb. Remove the cold pack 15 min before and during the dexrazoxane infusion (vasoconstriction reduces delivery). Topical DMSO is an alternative where dexrazoxane is not available; do not combine it with dexrazoxane. Vinca alkaloids: warmth and hyaluronidase. Intermittent warm compresses disperse and dilute the drug (the opposite of anthracyclines), plus hyaluronidase 150–1500 U SC around the site to aid dispersion. Cold is contraindicated. Mitomycin C and mitoxantrone: topical DMSO to the area, left to air-dry, repeated over several days. Grade There is no single severity scale. Management depends on the drug class (vesicant or irritant, and which vesicant), which decides compress temperature and antidote. Severity is then judged clinically from tissue changes over the following days: erythema, then blistering, then ulceration or necrosis. Disposition & escalation Surgical or plastic surgery referral for blistering, increasing pain, ulceration, or any large anthracycline extravasation despite dexrazoxane; debridement or reconstruction may be needed. Document fully, inform the treating team and complete an incident report; review with pharmacy before the next cycle (line choice, route of administration). Pitfalls Using the wrong temperature; cold for vinca alkaloids or warmth for anthracyclines worsens the injury. Anthracycline: cold. Vinca alkaloid: warm. Missing the 6-hour dexrazoxane window, or leaving the cold pack on during the infusion. Flushing the line or applying pressure; both spread the vesicant. Under-treating a central-line extravasation because the early signs are hidden. Pérez Fidalgo et al, ESMO-EONS Clinical Practice Guidelines, Ann Oncol 2012;23(Suppl 7):vii167 · Mouridsen et al (Savene TT01/TT02), Ann Oncol 2007;18:546 · Savene (dexrazoxane) EMA SmPC · ONS/ASCO extravasation guideline 2025. ESMO Handbook ch. on extravasation.

records.title: ICANS (immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity)
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Neurotoxicity after CAR-T or T-cell-engaging therapy: tremor, dysgraphia, expressive aphasia, reduced consciousness, seizures. Usually follows or overlaps CRS, days after infusion. Recognise: new tremor, word-finding difficulty or drowsiness after immune-effector-cell therapy. Expressive aphasia is the most specific early sign. Calculate the ICE score (0–10) and assign the ASTCT grade (see below). Corticosteroids are first line: dexamethasone, dose by grade; levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis and treatment. Tocilizumab does not treat ICANS (poor CNS penetration); use it only for concurrent CRS. Recognise Onset usually after or during CRS (rarely before), and can recur days later after CRS has settled. Typical sequence: tremor, dysgraphia, impaired attention and mild lethargy; then expressive aphasia (impaired naming, paraphasic errors, verbal perseveration); then depressed consciousness, and in severe cases seizures and cerebral oedema. Headache alone is not specific and is not ICANS. Exclude other causes of encephalopathy (sedatives, infection, metabolic causes, intracranial haemorrhage). Confirm ICE (Immune effector Cell-associated Encephalopathy) score, out of 10: Orientation (4): year, month, city, hospital (1 each). Naming (3): name 3 objects (for example point to clock, pen, button). Following commands (1): for example “show me 2 fingers”, “close your eyes and stick out your tongue”. Writing (1): write a standard sentence. Attention (1): count backwards from 100 by 10. Also assess level of consciousness, seizure activity, motor findings and signs of raised ICP regularly. Neurological observations, fundoscopy for papilloedema; low threshold for MRI brain and EEG (non-convulsive status), and LP when cerebral oedema or raised ICP is not suspected. Grade: ASTCT 2019 G1 ICE 7–9; wakes spontaneously. G2 ICE 3–6, or depressed consciousness, rousable to voice. G3 ICE 0–2, or rousable only to touch; any clinical or electrographic seizure that resolves; or focal or local cerebral oedema on imaging. G4 ICE 0 and unrousable (stupor or coma); prolonged (>5 min) or repeated seizures without return to baseline; deep focal motor weakness (hemiparesis or paraparesis); or signs of raised ICP or diffuse cerebral oedema (Cushing’s triad, papilloedema, CN VI palsy, decerebrate or decorticate posturing). The overall grade is set by the most severe domain; a normal ICE does not exclude high-grade ICANS if there is a seizure, raised ICP or deep motor weakness. In children <12, the CAPD replaces the ICE (score ≥9 = G3). Manage by grade Corticosteroids are the main treatment; start early rather than waiting for symptoms to peak. Doses follow the ASCO and NCCN algorithms: G1: supportive care and close monitoring; consider dexamethasone if not improving, especially with concurrent CRS. G2–3: dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 h (or methylprednisolone equivalent), tapered once improving. G4: high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g/day IV; ICU, airway protection, treatment of cerebral oedema and status epilepticus. Seizures: levetiracetam for prophylaxis and treatment; benzodiazepine, then further treatment for status; EEG for non-convulsive seizures. Concurrent CRS: tocilizumab with or without steroids for the CRS. Tocilizumab does not treat ICANS; it does not reach therapeutic CNS levels. Some protocols use anakinra for steroid-refractory ICANS. Disposition & escalation G1–2: monitored ward or HDU with frequent neurological observations according to the cellular-therapy protocol; G3–4: ICU. Notify the cellular-therapy team and follow the product and institutional pathway. Watch for concurrent CRS and for HLH or MAS. Neurology input for seizures, status or raised ICP. Pitfalls Giving tocilizumab for ICANS; it does not penetrate the CNS. Steroids are first line. Grading on the ICE alone and missing high-grade features (seizure, raised ICP, deep motor weakness). Attributing new drowsiness to sedatives and delaying steroids. Missing non-convulsive status; request an EEG for unexplained depressed consciousness. Related: CRS (this module); ICANS often follows or overlaps CRS, and tocilizumab given for CRS does not treat ICANS. Steroid doses by grade overlap the immunotherapy toxicity guidance in Tox.
