records.title: Severe immune-related adverse event crises
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Grade 3–4 checkpoint-inhibitor toxicities that are immediately life-threatening: myocarditis, colitis with risk of perforation, adrenal crisis, pneumonitis, encephalitis, myasthenia and myositis. Can present weeks to months after starting, and after stopping. Hold the checkpoint inhibitor and consider an irAE for any new organ dysfunction during or after ICI treatment; the diagnosis is easily missed. High-dose corticosteroids for grade 3–4 (typically methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day; 1 g/day IV for myocarditis). Early organ-specialist input (cardiology, gastroenterology, endocrinology, neurology, ICU). Not responding to steroids at 48–72 h: second-line immunosuppression (agent depends on the organ). Recognise Checkpoint-inhibitor toxicity can affect any organ, weeks to months after starting, and sometimes after the drug has stopped. The life-threatening presentations: Myocarditis: rare, but the irAE with the highest case fatality. New dyspnoea, chest pain, arrhythmia, heart failure; troponin rise, ECG changes. High mortality in early series. Colitis: high-volume or bloody diarrhoea; risk of toxic megacolon and perforation. Hypophysitis and adrenal crisis: fatigue, headache, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia; can present as circulatory collapse. Pneumonitis: dyspnoea, cough, hypoxia; can progress to respiratory failure. Neurological and neuromuscular: encephalitis; and a myasthenia, myositis and myocarditis overlap that can cause respiratory failure (monitor FVC and bulbar function). Confirm Urgent tests by organ. Myocarditis: troponin, ECG, echo, cardiac MRI, with or without biopsy. Colitis: stool infection screen, CT or flexible sigmoidoscopy. Endocrine: cortisol, ACTH, glucose, sodium, thyroid function, other pituitary axes. Pneumonitis: CT chest, exclude infection. Neurological: MRI, LP, EEG, and CK, repetitive nerve stimulation and anti-AChR antibodies for the myasthenia and myositis overlap. Always exclude infection and progression before attributing the picture to an irAE. Manage For all organs: hold the ICI, start high-dose corticosteroids, involve the organ specialist early, and move to second-line immunosuppression if there is no response to steroids at 48–72 h. By organ: Myocarditis: methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily (pulse), urgent cardiology, telemetry or ICU; if steroid-refractory, second-line treatment (for example MMF, ATG, abatacept, or tofacitinib on emerging data). Stop the ICI permanently. Colitis: methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day; if refractory or severe, infliximab 5 mg/kg, or vedolizumab 300 mg where infliximab is contraindicated (perforation, sepsis, untreated TB). Surgical review for perforation or megacolon. Hypophysitis and adrenal crisis: stress-dose hydrocortisone first (for example 100 mg IV, then 50 mg every 6 h, about 200 mg in 24 h) and fluids, before any thyroxine; giving thyroid hormone before cortisol can cause adrenal crisis. High-dose steroids do not reverse the endocrine deficiency; hormone replacement is usually lifelong. Pneumonitis: methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day, O₂, exclude infection; if refractory, infliximab, MMF or IVIG. Encephalitis, myasthenia and myositis: high-dose steroids plus IVIG or plasma exchange; monitor respiratory function (FVC, NIF) and intubate for neuromuscular respiratory failure. Avoid drugs that worsen myasthenia. Disposition & escalation Grade 3–4 irAEs need admission; myocarditis, neuromuscular respiratory compromise and adrenal crisis need ICU-level care. Involve the relevant specialist within hours. The decision on permanent discontinuation or later rechallenge is multidisciplinary; myocarditis and most grade 4 events mean permanent discontinuation. Once controlled, taper steroids slowly (≥4–6 weeks). Pitfalls Giving thyroxine before hydrocortisone in suspected hypopituitarism; this can cause adrenal crisis. Give cortisol first. Infliximab in ICI hepatitis; it is hepatotoxic and contraindicated. Use MMF. Under-dosing myocarditis; it needs pulse methylprednisolone (1 g), not 1 mg/kg. Attributing the picture to infection or progression and missing a treatable irAE, or the reverse; exclude infection before high-dose immunosuppression. Missing the myasthenia and myositis overlap until respiratory failure; monitor FVC early. Related: Tox has the full organ-by-organ irAE grading and management (CTCAE grades, prophylaxis, rechallenge); this card covers only acute grade 3–4 emergencies.
